title: Cuvier's Deep Dive: Ocean Zones
subtitle: Pilot the deepest-diving mammal on Earth and map the ocean's living layers.
module: High School — Module 4: Ocean Zones and Habitats

learningFocus.summary: Students map the ocean's vertical zonation — sunlight, twilight and midnight — by piloting a Cuvier's beaked whale and reading how light, temperature, pressure, salinity and dissolved oxygen change with depth. They practise the core Marine Science skill of relating living things to their abiotic conditions: distinguishing pelagic from benthic habitats, explaining why photosynthesis is confined to surface waters, and reasoning about the adaptations that let deep-sea organisms survive darkness, cold and immense pressure. It develops scientific enquiry (predict, observe, record, explain), analytical reading of a real oceanographic profile, and clear written communication of a cause-and-effect argument, tied directly to Module 4: Ocean Zones and Habitats.

orient.objective: Map how the ocean changes with depth — light, temperature and pressure — and explain how the life in each zone is adapted to the conditions there.
orient.courseLink: Marine Science, High School, Module 4: Ocean Zones and Habitats. It builds the zonation framework — pelagic and benthic, sunlight down to the hadal trenches — that later work on marine food webs, adaptation and human impact all rely on.
successCriteria: Name the ocean's zones in order of depth and state what happens to light, temperature and pressure as you descend.
Use your own dive data to explain why photosynthesis is limited to the surface waters.
Predict how a deep-sea organism is adapted to darkness, cold and high pressure, and justify each adaptation.
orient.mission: You are a Cuvier's beaked whale — the deepest-diving mammal on Earth. Dive from the sunlit surface toward the crushing dark near 3,000 m and record how the ocean changes beneath you. Your mission: map the living layers of the sea and work out how anything survives down there.
steps: Read the ocean-zones diagram, then predict what happens as you dive.
Pilot the whale down through the Sunlight, Twilight and Midnight zones.
Each new zone you reach logs its real conditions into your Investigation Record.
Explain the pattern, apply it to a new species, then take the Knowledge Check.
Generate your Learning Evidence to hand in.
orient.realLife: The ocean runs your life-support: its sunlit surface layer produces a large share of the oxygen you breathe, while the cold, dark deep stores carbon and feeds fisheries that hundreds of millions of people depend on.

predict.prompt: You are about to dive from the sunlit surface toward 3,000 m. As you go deeper, what will happen to the water temperature and the amount of light?
predict.hint: Think about how far sunlight can reach into water, and where the sun's warmth is added.

options.label: Both fall — it gets colder and darker
Both rise — it gets warmer and brighter
They stay about the same all the way down

investigate.title: Dive the Water Column
investigate.lede: W/S dive and rise, A/D steer, Shift to boost. Surface to breathe. Reach each new zone at least once — the moment you enter the Sunlight, Twilight, Midnight and seabed zones, its real temperature, pressure and light are logged to your Record below.

record.intro: Each ocean zone you reach logs its conditions here automatically — you never retype data the simulation already produced.
record.emptyText: No zones logged yet. Dive in the simulation to reach the Sunlight, Twilight and Midnight zones.

explain.prompt: Look at your Investigation Record. Describe how temperature and light changed as you dived from the Sunlight Zone to the Midnight Zone, and explain why almost no life in the deep ocean relies on photosynthesis.
explain.lede: Use the actual numbers from your dive.
expectedPoints: Temperature falls with depth (a warm surface layer then a sharp drop through the thermocline to near-freezing deep water).
Light falls rapidly and is effectively zero by about 1,000 m (the Midnight Zone is completely dark).
Photosynthesis needs light, so it can only happen in the sunlit surface layer; the deep sea instead depends on sinking marine snow, chemosynthesis or bioluminescent food webs.

apply.prompt: A newly discovered fish is caught at 2,500 m in the Midnight Zone. Using what you observed about the conditions there, predict TWO adaptations it is likely to have, and explain why each one helps it survive at that depth.
apply.lede: Base each adaptation on a specific condition you recorded — darkness, cold, or pressure.
expectedPoints: Bioluminescence or very large/sensitive eyes — to make or detect light in total darkness (to find prey, mates or camouflage).
A slow metabolism / ability to survive on little food — because food is scarce so far below the productive surface.
A body adapted to extreme pressure (no gas-filled swim bladder, flexible tissues) — pressure near 2,500 m is roughly 250 times that at the surface.
Dark or red colouration — camouflage in a zone where red light never reaches.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Which ocean zone receives no sunlight at all?
knowledgeCheck.explain: Below about 1,000 m no sunlight penetrates — the Midnight (Bathypelagic) Zone is in permanent darkness.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Roughly how much does water pressure increase for every 10 m you descend?

options.label: It does not change with depth

knowledgeCheck.explain: Every 10 m of water adds about 1 atmosphere, so at 3,000 m the pressure is around 300 atmospheres.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Match each ocean zone to what is found there.

pairs.right: Faint light; animals feed on marine snow
Total darkness lit only by bioluminescence

knowledgeCheck.explain: Light and food supply set what lives where: photosynthesis at the top, marine snow in the twilight, made-light in the dark, and chemical energy at the vents.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: In marine science, 'pelagic' describes life that lives…

options.label: in the open water, away from the seabed
on or buried in the seabed

knowledgeCheck.explain: Pelagic = the open water column; benthic = the seabed. A Cuvier's whale hunts in both.

rubric.note: You are graded out of the total marks, shown as a percentage.

criteria.label: Use of evidence
criteria.descriptor: Explain answer uses your own recorded dive data.

criteria.label: Scientific reasoning
criteria.descriptor: Apply answer links each adaptation to a specific condition.

criteria.label: Communication
criteria.descriptor: Clear sentences and correct marine-science terms.

aiMarkingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply) using the rubric and each question's expected_points. Copy auto_marked_score into knowledge_accuracy. Accept scientifically valid alternative wording and any two reasonable adaptations for Apply; do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Report the total, the percentage, one strength, one correction and one next step, all under 80 words.
